blocks.x: My name is W.R. Hogan. I'm chairman of the history department at Tulane University. And Mr. D. Clive Hardy of Tulane University staff and I are interviewing Mr. Nick LaRocca, the leader of the original Dixieland Jazz Band. Now my purpose in coming here to Mr. LaRocca's home is to sort of wind up the tape recordings which have been conducted over a period of some months. Mr. LaRocca has been ill and he's very kindly gotten up out of a sick bed in order to talk to us. The first questions I have arise out of some inquiries that came from a reading of Mr. LaRocca's tape recordings. And the first question has to do with his early life. In his statement about his father, he says that his father spoke four different languages. My first question is what four languages did he speak?

He spoke German, he spoke French, and Italian, and Portuguese. And he had trade with these boats, these nut boats, they were box. They were sailing vessels. At that time of my early life they had not no steamships. They had steamboats, but not steamships and the wharfs used to be open.
He needed these languages in his business.
That's correct. He used it to go in and do business with these people.
Now, Mr. LaRocca, did you ever personally learn any of these languages also?

No, I can't even speak Italian, but yet I can read the Italian newspaper and know what it's about and know every word about it, but I can't put it together. I never have tried, but all my sisters and brothers can speak it fluently. I was a boy that never stayed home much. I liked music and I traveled. Many of the times I would be out on the Gulf Coast playing when I was 15, 16, 17 years old out in Mississippi. And I'd travel along with different little groups of boys playing for what we could get in the early days.
Do you think that the fact that these languages were spoken in your home had any effect on your musical career?

No, I don't think so. My father played music, but he played conventional music off a book. He had a book where he used to make exercises. And maybe I got some of that stuff like in Ostrich Walk. That kind of exercises that I put into a tune later on, maybe. Being a faker now, you just don't pick up these things in one day. Maybe it hit you today and maybe it don't come out. Maybe in three, four months. First thing you know, you playing it.
Maybe ten years. Yes.
That's what I'm talking about. And you don't know where you got it from. And I don't say everything I made was exactly original, but the way I played it, it was original.
Sure. You mentioned White City in this manuscript. Where and what was White City?
Oh, that was in Chicago. That was in Chicago.
I got the impression it was some place around here.

No, they had no...oh, wait a minute. Stop the machine a minute. This was at Tulane Avenue in Carrollton. It was called the White City. They used to give plays there. Or semi-operatic plays and different things. My father used to take us there to listen to the music.
It was sort of a theater? Yeah, theater, yes.
And an amusement place. Oh, yeah. They had other things beside the theater. Then it became a ballpark years after. Oh, yes. That's where the main ballpark is. Yes, same ballpark.
You're in a motel now.
That's correct.
Now, tell us a little something about the amusement end of this. I'm personally interested in the amusements in the world.

Well, they used to have music in different little plays and shows like the burning of a city. Yeah. And you'd see a cardboard house that built and it had a fire. And some of the girls would hire for about $2 a night. And they'd come jumping out them windows. You understand? And that was bigger amusement to us. Then they had bands who'd play opera and singers. Real plays like they'd put on down there.
Did they serve beer or anything like that?

Well, they had all kinds of drinks. You could get anything you wanted. But my father didn't drink and he didn't bring us there. He always brought us where the soft drinks was. Yes. But they had other drinks around there also.
Did they have bottle soft drinks then?
Well, yes, they did. They had a small bottle with a rubber on it. And you'd push it up this way. They'd call it pop. Yeah.
That's what we call it pop.
Where the soda pop came down. Yeah. Pop. When you'd open it up, it would go pop.
Yeah.
And that's what they called pop. They had maybe cream soda and strawberry and maybe a pineapple. This was made there though.
Kind of like they're doing these.
No, these were bottles. They were bottles. Did they have a name on them?
Firm name?
Well, I couldn't.

Like Dr. Pepper? No, I couldn't tell you that. Now you're going way beyond me now. I couldn't go back that far and recreate that bottle. I can tell you the shape of the bottle. It wasn't exactly flat on the bottom. It was kind of round and it came up just the same as the other bottles. Yeah. If you ever look at one of these magnesia bottles in the old days about 15, 20 years ago, that was the style of bottle it was. I see.
Now, in the preceding tapes, I don't believe we've gone very much into your education. You went to school a while?

Yes, I went to St. Alphonsus' Parosal School. That's right down here, just about two blocks from here. Can you spell Alphonsus? A-L-P-H-O-N-S-U-S. Saint. S-T. Yes. And then when I finished there, I went to the university school that was run by Chenet and Dwyer.
How do you spell Chenet?
C-H-E-N-E-T. D-W-Y-E-R is the other man. And they had a man by the name of Perrin. Is this a private school?
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.

Oh, it was a private school. Yes. There was a preparatory school for people who went to going to other colleges. I was studying to go into Tulane to be a medical student. And my father died when I was 15 and a half, almost 16. And my mother couldn't keep up the tuition. And I was taken away from school.
Well, how far along, by modern standards, would you think that you got? Did you get well into high school?
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Oh, yes. I think I was in about two or three years in high school. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. But what I know today, them kids don't know when they come out of college.
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Yes. That's right. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Did you feel deprived when you had to abandon the idea of going into medicine as a career?

C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Well, I did sort of because I was in the same class with this Dr. Palmasana and I used to show him his lessons. He didn't know how to make his lessons. And I used to help him out. He used to live up here on a lean, I mean a magazine in Fusher, somewhere up in that neighborhood. But I think he's dead now, this man. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. He finally made it though. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Yes, he made it. He made it by the hardest. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.
Do you think of anything else in your early life that may have contributed to your musical career? That is, anything else that we haven't discussed?
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Well, I'll tell you what contributed more to my musical career because my daddy did want me to play and I want to play. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.
C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Because had he told me to study music, maybe I would have given it up.
That's the way I was. My mother's a music teacher.

Yeah, he told me to play the music, I would have given it up. But see, my inability to play music or to learn and nobody to teach me, yet my sisters all played. My brothers played. My older brother played violin. He played my notes. My two sisters, they played music.
Played piano?

No. One played a zitt and they all played by notes. They used to go around and sell these zitties with these things on. My father used to show them how to play. And at that time they used to play tunes like La Paloma. You don't hear them mention that at all. They'll tell you when the saints go marching in today. But they had numbers like Paloma over the waves mostly. I don't say all Italian music. But they were from all over. From Germany. From, I guess from every land in the world.
Did you ever have any musical groups get together and play or record? I don't mean record. I mean musical groups in your home that played together.

Well, yes. My sisters and brothers, my father played together but I never played. You never did play? No. No. I thought it was proud when I first learned the cornet. It was his cornet that I used to take down the empty house. Well, he lived at that time at Washington Avenue, St. Thomas. Down in the next block was an empty house. I used to go down there and play his horn. In other words, take it without him knowing. Not steal it because I'd bring it back and play. And I thought I'd learned a few tunes by writing the numbers down on what valves to press in. I went home and played the number. And when I did bingo's a horn, he chopped it up with the axe, his own horn. He told me all musicians was tramps. And today I have an idea that he was somewhere near right.
Was he right about most musicians in that day?
Well, at that time, you see, when he came here, he thought he could make a living on music.
I see.

And he couldn't make a living in music. He had to do other things besides playing music. Because most of the people that hired you then for a birthday party, something got you for nothing. They got a group of musicians together and that's all. You got food and drink and that's all you got. There was nothing to take home.
Mr. Marocca, did you ever play, or not play, but sing or have anything to do with the St. Alphonsus choir?

No, I didn't. But I did sing at the closing exercise. And there was a man who used to teach us there, was named Sokola. His first name, I can't remember. But he used to put on the show for us. And we were singing the Holy City. Ta-da, ta-da, ta-da, ta-da, Hosanna, and so on. And I used to sing counter melodies against it. At that time I didn't know anything. I could show you on the piano how easy it is for me to get a melody. And many people say, how you put them together? Well, to me they come just like they come out the air. All I need is four notes or five notes to start on. And a chord construction to follow. And I can make a melody. And that's not only now. I've been doing that since I've been nine, ten years old. You've just published a couple of rec...
Yes.

...piece of sheet of sheet of sheet. And I had good luck on one of them. This last group. Yes. I put that with Charles H. Hanson Music Publishers. And he'll take more if I put them on tape. He's looking for original music of Nick LaRocca. And I couldn't tell you more on that. You've got some more. Oh yes. I've got about 40, 50 numbers. I have 25 of them I just had copyrighted in the last year. 25 copyrighted?
Yes.

Within the last year? Within the last year. And I have 25 others that is not copyrighted. Then I have about 30 or 40 of them that has no copyright that I've had laying in the drawer for me. Many, many years. Many of them. I had men like Eugene West used to come to me for melodies. And I'd give them songs. And when they come out they were different. I'll show you in a pack right here. I give them a song and it was called Once In A While. And then they changed the title. And what you think they did, they took the title and put it on their song. And made my song, Summer In A Night. And this song went for a hit. And mine stood there, Summer In A Night.
I don't know. Do you have any pieces among the ones that you haven't published, which might be described as jazz pieces in the sense that Tiger Rag and pieces like that?

Yes, I've got others. I don't see it as good as Tiger Rag, but there's one in here that has a very good jazz number. And this Let's Jam It has plausibilities. Even this one that I put out as a popular number can be played in the same idiom that I would play it. And so on. There's nothing to it. Any tune becomes a jazz tune when you put the idioms to it. 된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된

These people tell you it's a great big secret. It's nothing but march time, syncopated. White man's music and not colored. That's all it is. You take the tiger rank, we'll fit in that. You play. Hold that tiger. Hold that tiger. You can do anything you want with it. It's waking up different embellishments on a chord construction. That's all it is. Now these fellas in New Orleans, they play today. You know who they play? I'm going to let you know who they play. They're great. I was nobody. They play Big Spider-Back. They play Red Nichols. And they play Bonnie Berrigan. And if you don't believe what I tell you, they play the three of them together. And so all of them copied from Nick LaRock and admitted. In fact, I started Big Spider-Back on the horn. And you must study his records and listen to his endings. And he developed a style of music. That's from the ostrich walk. The same as Louis Armstrong's attack. And the same as the rest of them modern men who'd taken from the records, which they had something to work on. I didn't. All I had was ragtime music that was played by note to play with. And I had to make my own. And these fellas had something to work with. And it's an easy thing when you can lay out on record and play alongside of it. You can play a contra melody. You can play against it. And you can make up your own style when you have something already started for you.

Mr. LaRock, I'm glad you brought Big's name into this. Because I wanted you to tell us a little more about your relationship with him. In your previous statement, you said you thought he was a very great musician.
Yes. I still think that. But he played piano when I first met. He was a young boy.
Where was that?
In Rising Web. It was about the latter part of 1918.
You've told about that on the tape.
Yeah, it was just about to finish. And he left the high school and came up there. And in 1923 he came back again. And I used to let him sit in with me and play in the band.
And then sit down. You'd actually sit there and play?
Yes, sit in the back of me.
And he'd play along with you? Along with me, yes.

And you had two trumpets then? Two trumpets. He played a second. He was a very good harmonist. He was very fast on the catch on the ear. He played piano, but not a jazz piano. I never heard him play on a record, but I did hear him. In 1923 he sat down. And he knew all operatic tunes. He was taught that. He was taught by music. But he became a faker on the carnet. Now that's about all I could tell you outside when he came down here with Whiteman in 1926. I renewed my, or 25, 26, I don't know the exact date because. Came to New Orleans? Yes, they came here with Whiteman at the Tulane University Stadium. And he played a concert there, Paul Whiteman.
Did you hear it?
Oh yes, I was there.
What did you think about it?

I thought it was all right, but Whiteman never played no jazz. He'd taken all the arrangements from the Dixieland Jazz Band. It don't take you long to hear that. Go listen to his wang wang blues. Or any tunes that Bussie played. Bussie made this little lick that Joe Oliver made before Joe Oliver put it on the record. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Joe, if you don't believe it, listen to Hot Lips Bussie playing on Hot Lips.
That's his favorite piece. I've heard him many times. All right. The dance touch.
Now you'll hear that same idiom that Joe Oliver uses in there.
You think Bussie invented this?
Yeah, he invented it. No, he got it from me.
Oh yes.

That's where he got it. They all got it. None of them. They're not none of them. Invented, none of that stuff. That's where they taken it from. The original Dixieland Jazz Band recording. Bussie used to sit up at Rice and Webber's there when he was out of a job. He used to almost cry. Ted Lewis was another one.
They would come in and listen to you.

Yes. Sit up in the lobby. They wasn't working. They'd sit up there and listen. Why would he almost cry? Well, because he was out of a job. Oh. And at that time when that music was changing and they had to have something to work that was before the record. After the record was out there, many of them came there. It's been said that many of these colored men preceded us up there. Because I don't know about that. I couldn't comment. But I can tell you one band that didn't precede us to New York. That was the Creole band and they came March the 6th. And if you don't want to look up the New York papers, you can see what I tell is the truth. And they're recorded like Brian Russ found. He found the dates that I give him were correct.
Well, Mr. Broome found the same thing in Chicago. Yes, sir.
And you find everything that I tell you has been right.
Now, could you tell us a little about your impressions of Bix Beiderbeck as a person? What kind of personality did he have?
Well, he was a, I'd say, you see this young man here?
Sure.

Now, I won't put him in his class because I don't think he'd go as far as Bix went. But he was a very quiet man. Sure. Quiet mannerism. Quiet fellow. Very, very quiet. And what he did later years, well, I got no comment on that because I had no business even talk about it.
But you liked him personally.
Personally, I thought he was a wonderful boy. And there was nothing I wouldn't do for him or help him if I could. At that time, in the beginning of the music.
If he had lasted, of course, he died very young. Yes. If he had lasted, do you think he would have continued to be a great musician, gotten better? Had he already reached his peak when he died?

Well, I couldn't tell you on that because, you know, every man has his own given powers and the limits of how far he can go. But most of the tunes that he copied, he copied from the original Dixieland jazz band. Most of them that he recorded was recorded before him by the original Dixieland jazz band.
I think he said this, hadn't he, somewhere? Yes. He said he studied your records?

Yes. That's all he ever knew was original Dixieland jazz band music. But he tried to build his style the same as Napoleon, Red Norval, Red Nichols. All these fellas tried to make up a different style of their own, to be a little different. They added to it, and what it is today, it ain't what we played. It's nowhere near it, because you can listen to our records. I don't say we great musicians, but we only knew playing harmony. Today they use more modern harmony, and they got better technique, and they taught in school the music, which I never had that chance, and I never was given that chance. But I'm glad, in a way, I wasn't given that chance, because probably I wouldn't be here talking. I'd be still like the rest of them.
I've known people who had classical training who never could learn to play jazz.
That's right.
Particularly on the piano.
That's right. They just can't make it. They just don't feel it. They don't have it. And that's all I can tell you on that part of it.

Now, I would like for you to tell me what your impressions of the use of the word jazz is. When did you first hear this word? Did you ever hear it in New Orleans before you went north? How did it first enter into your consciousness?
Well, I never heard of the word jazz in New Orleans. I never knew what the word jazz meant. After I was in Chicago, about a week, a couple kept hollering, jazz it up, jazz it up, jazz it up.
Give us some more jazz. There's people out in the audience.
That's right, on the dance floor.
I see. You never heard it before then?
No, sir. I never heard of it. I never heard it being used.
This word wasn't used in connection with your band up to that time?
No, it wasn't used in connection with the band in the beginning.
Yeah.

No, the first advertisement was never in connection with the band at all. The word was put on after by Harry James. And after they had so many New Orleans boys come up there, everybody was called a New Orleans jazz band after our band was called jazz. Now, I later found out that the word came from the underworld or meant something bad.
Probably in Chicago. In Chicago. In Chicago.
In that area, yes. Around 22nd Street, 14th Street. We had these bad women hanging around. They used that word.
You don't know how far the word went back before that, though.

Oh, no. It could have been gone for years before I knew it. I wouldn't say that that was the first time it was used because I'd be telling a lie. I wouldn't know nothing about that. But the first time I ever heard it, when it was a first called out in front of the band, then Mr. James advertised us as a jazz band.
It was his idea.
That's right.
He was sort of a manager, entrepreneur. Impressor. Yeah.
Yeah, he was a manager.
Impressorio.
Impressorio, whatever you call it. You correct me in my English because I don't know good English. I try anyhow. I think your English is pretty good.
Then, after that, the word caught on pretty rapidly all over the country.

No, not that fast. Yeah. No, it didn't caught on that fast. It was the records that had worldwide distribution that went as far as Honolulu, Germany, Japan. If you look up my clippings, you'll find they had a jazz club in Japan in 1919. Look, they only got a jazz club in New Orleans in 1949. That's funny, ain't it? 30 years after Japan has a jazz club. They built a New Orleans jazz club. And this man becomes a historian.

Now, one of the things that I'm personally interested in is the way the public, or certain aspects of the public, the way the press, or certain aspects of the press, opposed jazz in the beginning. They thought it was not something that ought to be encouraged.
No, it didn't.
Now, would you care to comment on the whole history of the way jazz finally got to be adopted?
Well.
A respectable sort of thing.

When we went to New York and we made a great big hit, the word jazz was accepted as a respectable word, as the people didn't know what it meant. First, the Victor Company put the first record out, J-A-S-S. They had four different ways of spelling jazz. Believe it or not, the first way to spell it, J-A-S, I claim none of it. That's my second name. It was the abbreviation of James. I never knew. And I have never claimed it up to today because it never was meant for me because nobody knew my name was jazz in Chicago. After the Victor Company put the Circular's out, these records had worldwide distribution. And they went all over the country. stuff people here in Times-Picayune wrote an article called Jazz and Jazzism which you would contain at your archives.
They spelled it with a double S.

Double S. Now let me tell you how many spellings they had and you can find them. They had J-A-S J-A-S J-A-S-Z around in the 15th and we arrived in New York and we tried out two weeks. Many people think we started on the 26th or 27th. That's not right. We were there before the 7th because we didn't have no uniforms to work with and we went over to Jimmy Balletta's and Nat Levy to get tuxedos fitted up for us and make us look like gentlemen. Now we're coming out of a dive in Chicago and we're going into first class place, one of the largest places in New York and we tried out the Coconut Grove. We tried out at the Paradise. We tried out at the 400 room. We played in the main dining room. All these places we played before we had a contract. And in the paper around the 15th you will find in the telegram J-A-S-Z. They spelled it. J-A-S-Z. They spelled it.

but that ain't the way we give it to them. We spell it J-A to bless. Well, I'm running ahead on something here. The Victor Company first spell it J-A to bless. Then they change it J-A-Z-Z. Some of the young fellas are going with girls, and they take off the J off the front, rub it off with a knife. And they say, you want to hear some good music? Look at the title of that thing. And it was a vulgar word then. It became a vulgar word. It always was a vulgar word to me because that's what I knew it is to be. And our music had that same effect on the dancers. In other words, a lot of people say that we didn't do nothing. They go around and they tell you, oh, this man did this, this one did that. They tell you when they close the district down, that's when they spread jazz. That's not so. Jazz had spread before Joe Oliver came. And not only that, when Joe Oliver made them records, he had young men with him who copied from the Dixieland band. And if anyone cares, listen, I've studied them records. And they're taking Shields part in total. And they're taking part of my first cornet part on the Leverstable Luce. Johnny Dodd uses that.
Mr. Rocca, all during the 20s, and to some extent during the 1930s, there were people who were deriding jazz who said it was something
that we ought to try to abolish.

Etude magazine carried long discourses about how this was such an awful kind of music. What do you think the sum total effect of jazz upon life in the United States and our influence abroad has been? Do you think it's been for the good or the bad?

Well, the music itself didn't make the people bad. It gave them a sort of enjoyment. In other words, many masters have strived to move people. It took this music to move them. But you don't mention the times Picayune who started all this thing down the road, then was taken up by the dancing masters of Chicago. Then in 1920, John Roach Stanton had a bill passed. Up to this time, there were no Negro bands playing jazz, only imitators.
That was a New York minister.

Yeah, a New York minister. He went to Albany and knocked us out of a job, forcing us relegated to a dance hall. We took the job in the dance hall. That almost took all the starch out of me. The Victor Company refused to record any more jazz. They made us put a saxophone in the band, and this thing almost ruined the band. Never gave us the right, although, write kind of music. Although this man was a wonderful musician, he was a very talented musician, Benny Kruger. But nobody wanted to record jazz no more, only the okay people. Well, we went to the okay people and recorded two numbers, or two different sittings, I think four numbers all together. And they come out in their little book, and they call it race records, making Negroes out of us. And then that's why I quit them. And we had no place else to record. Nobody wanted jazz. Everybody was against it. Whiteman had come in, and he sweetened the style. He didn't play jazz. He called himself the king of jazz. But he didn't play no jazz. You've got his records to go by, you can see. See what I say is, I have been telling what is being the truth, and not bumped up from memory, like these people took this Negro to Washington with jugs of wine. I've been told by someone that heard the record, and he says, I like whiskey. Give me some more whiskey on the record. That's a wonderful thing to put out by the State Department, or by anyone that wants to put that out.
Who was this?

A Jelly Roll Martin. Oh, yeah. It's on the record, where he says, you can hear him say, I like whiskey. Give me some more whiskey. This fellow invented him. This man never was recognized in his life. You mean Alan Lomax. Alan Lomax invented him.
Did you ever see Jelly Roll Martin?

No, I never knew him. I never met him. In fact, I never knew Joe Oliver. I never met Pompous Celestine to La New Orleans Jazz Club down here, and Miss Menville introduced me to him. And she asked him, was this one of the men who used to sit down and listen to you? He said, no, ma'am. I never seen this man in my life before. I had already told her I never met him, but she didn't believe it, but she tried to put me on the spot. But that Negro had more honesty and truthfulness in his body than Miss Menville has in her whole family. He told her right there and then. He said, no, I never seen this man in my life before. And I told her, I thank you, Celestine, for telling the truth because there's been many lies that's been told around New Orleans. What else do you want to ask?
Was Celestine playing when you were a young man?

No. They say he was playing. I couldn't tell you. Some people say he played down in the district. Maybe he was. But when I went down there, I didn't have that kind of money to go in a dance hall. We went down there with our 50 cents. We went to the Greenwald Theater first to look at the girls' show, Burla's show. Then we'd make it back there. We didn't go in where they was dancing because you'd have to have money to go and dance with them women. You couldn't go in them places without money.
Taxi dance hall.
Yeah. Yeah, no. Yeah. From what I understood, you'd go in there and you'd meet a girl and you'd buy beer or highballs and you'd pay for it.
Yeah.

And maybe cost you 10, 15, 20 dollars before you got out of there. And I only had 50 cents to spend. Sure. And I spent that 50 cents and I got out of there because it wasn't a place for any decent man to hang around.
I want to change the subject. This album here is a recording of the record you made in Great Britain in 1919.
I understand another one has been issued. Yes, sir. Well, there are two of them at least that have been reissued. Yes.
Now, is there any one place or any one set of albums or records that is available in this country that has most of your original records available for people who like to buy them?

No. You see, the thing is these people control the press. they control the television. I've been fighting these television people for a long time. If you care to look up my things, letters that I wrote and tell them about the lies they were fouling up the air with filthy lies and propaganda. No.
My point is don't you think it'd be a good idea if somebody could be persuaded to bring all your original records in an album?
Yes, it would be a good idea. It would be a good idea. But who's going to do it?
Well, here they're doing it in England.
That's right.
And I think possibly your best records are made on this side.

On this side. The Victor's got the best records and the Victor company, I asked them for permission to re-dub them records and they told me that they come from their legal department that they kept them in their vault. They called them some kind of record vault. And my hands was tied. I was going to take a chance and put them out myself to combat this propaganda that these other men were putting out. You see, they have an organization that make money at this thing called the Jazz Club. The very word they use is stolen from the Dixeland jazz band who made this word famous around the world. Marshall Stearns, you look up his articles in Downbeat in 1936, he says, we ought to find a different expression than jazz for the music because when you say jazz, it pertains to anything from the Dixeland band to Paul Whiteman. That's what Marshall Stearns had. He tried to change the name. They tried to call it Chicago Swing. They tried to call it everything. In 1936, I went and brought the band back and we still kept it jazz. They never changed nothing. And they couldn't sell it as anything else because too many people know about it. And it won't be just a question of time that these people will have to tell the truth. Just recently, I got a thing from Leonard Feather. first time in my life anybody wrote me anything to find out about me to print. In all these years that I've been around, I have never had one of these jazz historians ask me one question about jazz. But they go ask other guys who never was around and never made a success about it. They say, I want to take everything from myself. I never.
Did you answer his inquiry?

Yes, I did. He says he's building up a new, what do you call it, on jazz. And what did I do since 1955? He don't ask me what I did before. But I took the liberty of telling him where to look for the true history on jazz and stopped writing his filthy lies. And I says, I don't have many days on this earth. and I hope to see some truth before I die be printed about jazz music.
Have you heard from him?
No, he has never. I sent him two pieces of music to.
He didn't acknowledge you.

No, he never acknowledged nothing. He's supposed to help that German man along. in the jazz history. They were going to put down on a moving picture, take names and places of jazz history. And all you can get out of them people is the music come from Africa. It's like I seen Sushan get on the television one day. I'm sitting right in this kitchen here. and he says, I went all the way to the wires of Africa. endangered my health, he says, to get the rhythm. And he says, of course, I could play many other jazz records, but I'm kind of selfish. I'm going to play one of my own, he says. And he goes on there and he plays that crummy banjo guitar he's got. Now, this man never was a musician in my days. Probably couldn't make a living at his doctor business. He's got a brother and there's a lawyer and I want him to hear what I have to say. He said many dirty things about me through other people's name put to it. I have never said anything dirty about him, anybody else. But when it was time to prove it, these men ran just like he'll run. He says, he puts articles in the second line. That's the books you must read. They have a man that came down here when the New Orleans Jazz Club was formed, named by a carpet bagger in other words, a northern carpet bagger by the name of Dave Stein. Whether it's related to the Stein's Edgar Stein or not, I don't know. I don't
think so.

Maybe I'll get in trouble by mentioning Edgar Stein but he put money in there. But this Edgar Stein had a lot to do from keeping me from getting recognition because he was a big owner in the times, picking on a long time ago. And I found out all this stuff, not recently, but in a roundabout way, things have been rounding themselves up. this Dave Stein came here, he bought the New Orleans item in. He was the same man who created the talking mule, Francis. He helped to create the talking jackasses, the New Orleans jazz club, where he lent them Thomas sanctioned to go around the crazy house to find out about Buddy Bowling. then later they dug up Bowling's grave to see if they could find an autograph of some tune that he made, maybe buried alongside of him, that he could get up and autograph a piece for Miss Myra Mendel because she's got all the autographs of all the other musicians, all the other great Negro musicians she has. This is the same man that whenever any Negro died, he was a great jazz man. stuff stuff

Aided in a better by no other than Dr. Sushant, who puts himself as a jazz historian. Now this man here, as a jazz historian, never played jazz. He says he used to sit across the road from on Basin Street and listen to Joe Oliver playing music. And there's where he got his idea from. Well now the only thing he could have heard on Basin Street, and there's many more men as old as I am, can tell you they had no music on Basin Street outside a little violin or a piano. Or they had three Negro Rhymers at Anderson's. But Joe Oliver, you couldn't hear him on Basin Street. The only thing he could have been counting was the customers who went into Lula White's or Josie Arlington's. And that's all. And he says he went over to get a beer and some of his articles. Well I can tell you this. New Orleans was a place less than 285,000 people. There wasn't a police that wasn't on every block, that knew every strange face that come into the district. He'd have had his tail whipped with the strap because they don't play with them like they play with them today. They played with them as gentlemen. Them police worked on you. You were bad, they made you good. There was no two ways about it. And you could tell your daddy when you went home you got another beating too. But today the daddy wants you to put police in jail for whipping a bad boy. That's why you have so much damn juvenile delinquency and all other stuff around this country. Through propaganda. Through lies that's been spread around. You don't know what to believe anymore. But getting back to the jazz club these people formed a racket. Marshall Stern founded a good racket. He got any milk. The Guggenheimer Foundation on it. Got a lot of money. I don't know whether he divided it up with Dr. Sushon or not. But up to that time Dr. Sushon was with me. You got his letter to Lane. He says notwithstanding he says the original Dix-Lane jazz band started the whole thing. Today I didn't start anything. I was nowhere around. He was around with his six and seven eight band. They make me laugh sometime. To get on here with his colored funerals. I feel sorry for colored man. I say give him what any white man deserves. A good living. A good job. Good education. But when it comes to integration. They may be hard on me on this. But I say I draw the line. Because he hasn't earned that in their morals. Now they have some good colored people. They don't suffer. They're allowed to make a good living. As any white man. As people run insurance companies. As the Gieders. And Moss. And other people. Who set themselves up in business. I had many colored people work with me. And they used to bring up this subject. I said now what stopped you from building a hotel for colored people. As well as a white man building a hotel for white men. Why do you want an extra to a white man? Well it says that's equality. No that ain't equality. I say. Do you think it's equality that I can't go down in one of these big clubs? I'm a white man. I'm bored from their clubs. I can't get in their clubs. That's segregation against me. I don't have no scruples against that. First place I don't have the money. Next place I don't belong in there. I'm a poor man. They're rich men. And when the colored man says he's the same as the white man. I say it's wrong. Because when I read a lot of these guys. And they went track back to Europe. To Africa. All they found. Yes they found where white men were. That they had some of them were smart. And just like a beggar. When you put them on a horse. They want to ride them to death. But I say the NACP is riding to a great big fall. And it ain't going to be long either. Because they will never get integration. The way they want it. They want white skin. They don't want equality. They want to marry. With white people. Now. That's allowed to be done. I feel sorry for the Anglo-Saxon people. And the European white people. What you call the Caucasian race. Because two thirds of the world. Are yellow and black. You won't have no white race. I was once told by a doctor. He said Mr. La Rocca. You're a holler at that colored man. He says you'll save yourself. You're going to get heart trouble. He says you've got a million years of learning you. This Negro has 150 years of education behind him. How can a brain compete with a man. That has millions of years. Of cultivation of ideas. And this colored man just has in the last 150 years. A little education that he has acquired from the white man. Compete with him. Yes there's plenty of smart colored men. But I haven't seen no Enrico Fermi. I haven't seen no Einstein with him. I ain't seen no Columbus. Not coming out of Africa. And if you want to know the truth about her. I ain't never been to Africa. They don't have no jazz music there either. They don't have no Dixieland music. They never had no instruments there either. And they don't even know where the wheel is. They're so damn lazy. All they do is lay down and let the women work for them. And when they come over here. That's what they expect to do. Get the women to work for them. And that's what they do here. Their women work for them. Can I put something else on there? I'm going out of line now.
Go ahead.
Whatever you want.
That's why I came down here.

Yeah right sir. I want to talk about. In my work in Carpenter work. I went to many places. They had many colored people. I used to see a lot of colored children. And one family had so many different names. I said how comes his name. Well his father left me. He's disappeared. Well I said how you support him. You don't work. She says well I get relief. Fifty dollars a month for each child. That's a hell of a good racket. They can propagate like rats. White woman. Go there. She'll turn red in the face. You go down to charity hospital. I've been told white people. I never went. I never had occasion to. But I have had a brother went there. And they turn him down. He didn't have no money. But they don't turn the negro down. Somehow or another they feel sorry for him. Poor colored man. You can't see the reaction on his face. But if I tell you a lie. You're going to see it on my face. I'm going to turn red. And you're going to catch me in that lie. But you don't catch the negro in a lie. Because he don't have that. He makes believe he's stupid. He ain't stupid. He's smart. And the same one with these women. That they have. And nine-tenths of the colored people. They don't marry. They live together. And any white person that says that they fit. To integrate. I see. They're stepping down. And lowering the morals of the white race. All you have to do is read Louis Armstrong's book. He had nine daddies. He says he didn't know who was his right daddy. He didn't know. But he had nine daddies. That's what they're trying to force on you. These minority groups. They tell you. That integration is good. It's the right thing to do. But. These people themselves. I won't mention. They came here in around 1600. I've studied them. Studied them very good. They disappeared. As the same people. And they come back. And they emerge. And they're all the same people. Yet they have never integrated. But the Italians. The Germans. The Frenchmen. The selectors of Raco. The selectors. Or any other nationality. They intermarry. But. This one kind of people. They don't. They don't mix. But they tell. And how to run the country. And the countries run according to that. They control the money. They control the television. They control all the big presses. And that's the way it goes. And they want integration. But. White man has no more to say anymore. About integration. Because those rights have been taken away from him. By a supreme court. Men I guess. Who never were judges any more than I am. That don't know anything. I am in favor of giving every colored man. His just dues. And let him remain colored. The same as he's been. Build hotels for him. Build everything for him. Schools. Give him college education. If he wants it. Now if anybody's got any grievance against me. That'd be just too bad for me. Because. I. I want to make this tape. And I want. My expression. To be on that tape. Just as it is. I'm a segregationist. And a die hard one. Because I don't think. The colored man has joined this place. So far. Maybe years to come. Yes. But not now. Any other questions? Any other questions?
Hello.

segments.title: Father's languages and music, and where La Rocca's style came from
segments.summary: La Rocca recalls his father's multilingual trade and conventional music; he himself traveled and played on the Gulf Coast, and says his ideas came from absorbed exercises but his playing was original.

segments.title: White City amusement park on Tulane Avenue
segments.summary: He clarifies that White City was a theater and amusement place in Carrollton where his father took the family, later the ballpark site.

segments.title: Shows, drinks and bottled pop at White City
segments.summary: Hogan asks about the amusements; La Rocca describes burning-city shows, opera bands, soft drinks and the old pop bottles.

segments.title: St. Alphonsus school and leaving the prep school after his father's death
segments.summary: He describes his schooling, the private school he left at 15 when his father died, and abandoned medical plans; the spelling of the school name loops in ASR.

segments.title: Father's attitude to music and the family's zither playing
segments.summary: La Rocca says his father pushing him might have made him quit; his siblings played by notes, including zithers and tunes like La Paloma.

segments.title: Taking his father's cornet and why music paid so little
segments.summary: He secretly practiced on his father's cornet, which his father chopped up, calling musicians tramps; musicians then earned only food and drink.

segments.title: Singing at St. Alphonsus closing exercises
segments.summary: Asked about the choir, he says he sang counter-melodies to The Holy City at school closing exercises under a teacher named Sokola.

segments.title: His unpublished compositions and what makes a tune jazz
segments.summary: La Rocca talks about his recently copyrighted numbers, a publisher, a song idea taken by others, and says any tune becomes jazz with the idiom applied.

segments.title: Claims that Bix, Red Nichols and Berigan copied the Original Dixieland Jazz Band
segments.summary: He says New Orleans players now imitate Bix, Nichols and Berigan, who in turn copied him, and that later men had records to work from.

segments.chapter: Bix, Whiteman and the copying claim
segments.title: Meeting Bix Beiderbecke and letting him sit in
segments.summary: La Rocca recalls meeting the young Bix on piano in Chicago in 1918, and letting him play second trumpet with the band in 1923.

segments.chapter: Bix, Whiteman and the copying claim
segments.title: Paul Whiteman's concert and the claim that others took ODJB licks
segments.summary: Discussing Whiteman's 1926 New Orleans concert, he says Whiteman, Busse and Joe Oliver took arrangements and licks from the Dixieland band, whose records musicians gathered at Reisenweber's to hear.

segments.chapter: Bix, Whiteman and the copying claim
segments.title: Bix's personality and his debt to ODJB records
segments.summary: He describes Bix as quiet and likeable, says Bix learned only from the band's records, and that today's style is far from what they played. He and Hogan agree classically trained pianists often cannot play jazz.

segments.chapter: The word jazz and the band's New York success
segments.title: First hearing the word jazz in Chicago and Harry James
segments.summary: La Rocca says he first heard the word jazz in Chicago, that manager Harry James put it on the band, and that it had underworld associations.

segments.chapter: The word jazz and the band's New York success
segments.title: How the word spread, and Japan's 1919 jazz club
segments.summary: He says records, not the word, spread jazz worldwide, noting a jazz club in Japan in 1919 and New Orleans only in 1949.

segments.chapter: The word jazz and the band's New York success
segments.title: Spellings of jazz on Victor records and the New York tryout
segments.summary: He discusses the varied spellings of jazz on early Victor releases, the New York tryouts before the contract, and how the word turned vulgar.

segments.title: Opposition to jazz, Rev. Stanton, and the band's decline
segments.summary: Asked about critics of jazz, La Rocca blames a New York minister for costing the band its job, Victor dropping jazz, and Whiteman sweetening it.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton, Joe Oliver and Celestin, and the district dance halls
segments.summary: He says he never met Morton, Oliver or Celestin and describes visiting the district with 50 cents and avoiding the taxi dance halls.

segments.title: Reissues of his records and Victor's refusal
segments.summary: Hogan shows a British reissue; La Rocca complains about media control and says Victor refused to let him re-dub the originals.

segments.title: Feud with jazz historians, the New Orleans Jazz Club and Stein
segments.summary: He describes a reply to a jazz-history writer, attacks Dr. Souchon and Africa-origin claims, and blames Edgar and Dave Stein for blocking his recognition.

segments.title: Disputing Souchon's claims of hearing Joe Oliver on Basin Street
segments.summary: He says no music like that was on Basin Street and goes on to complain about police, discipline and juvenile delinquency.

segments.title: Segregationist monologue and ending the tape
segments.summary: La Rocca delivers a long statement against integration and states he is a die-hard segregationist before the tape closes.
